rv.q: They are an army of only two, yet they seem destined to conquer and slay anyone who ventures into the Lyceum Theater, where they have set up their festering — and, admit it, stupendously entertaining — camp.
It's devotion well-earned, because these comedians... have sharpened to a very funny point an acumen for keeping an audience off-balance - and eager for more.
Even ones that shouldn’t kill do, like a description of “one of those large, New York City diners where even the ice cream is bad”
What makes 'Oh, Hello' work so well is that Messrs. Kroll and Mulaney have created a pair of genuinely funny characters who are more than mere collections of tics and catch phrases.
Not to mention the funniest show in town.
It’s hard not to laugh at the running motif of their affected mispronunciation of ordinary words, like dialorg and Broadway, with a strong emphasis on the second syllable.
“Oh, Hello on Broadway” might not be the show to win over new enthusiasts.

The show, iterations of which have been enthusiastically embraced on the road and Off-Broadway, bungees around with absurd, occasional cleverness, with dated references to Blue Man Group and softball observations about theater cliches.
They make mustiness new, and they're a New York City must.

You're there to see Kroll and Mulaney's masterful take on the Faizon and St. Geegland — two incredibly nuanced and well-rounded characters who manage to be wildly offensive and incredibly loveable at the same time.

It's a sketch, drawn out. What's actually most interesting, if not really explored, is Kroll and Mulaney's obvious love for theater, through their jokes about recurring dramatic devices - the one-sided phone call, the bloody handkerchief that indicates imminent death, the profound curtain line - and bits of shtick about other plays.
As staged by Alex Timbers (the freethinking director behind “Peter and the Starcatcher” and “Andrew Jackson”), “Oh, Hello” is 95 minutes of politically incorrect, gleefully silly fun.
There are moments that had me in stitches, but the show’s so shapeless and shaggy that it doesn’t add up to much.
But it starts out funny and moves past hysterical to sublime.
But, over 95 minutes, there is also a fair share of clunkers, bottom-drawer lines such as a reference to "Tennessee Williams and his sister Serena."
The big problem with “Oh, Hello on Broadway,” which opened Monday at the Lyceum Theatre in New York, is that Mulaney doesn’t deliver.
It was worth every drop of blue ink that I aquired.
I was surprised at how little I laughed during Oh, Hello on Broadway, a comedy act by Nick Kroll and John Mulaney.
